add/problem: Walking back along a chain, you multiply by one local slope per link. But a node in a graph can take two inputs, so walking back through it raises a question: how much of the slope goes to each input?
add/gate: Take an add. Going forward, it adds x, three, and z, minus four, to make q, minus one. Then q flows on, through the rest of the graph, to its final output, f.
add/name: Nodes like this are also called gates, after the gates of an electronic circuit: small parts that each take a couple of inputs, and send out one.
add/above: Say the walk back has already reached q. Nudge q up by a hundredth, and f moves up two hundredths: two per unit of q.
add/up: That rate is the gradient of f with respect to q, written partial f, partial q: here, two. It arrives from above, from the output's side, and the code calls it d q.
add/curly: Why the curly d? f depends on many inputs, so its slope in q holds all the others still: a partial derivative. In a chain with one input, like d z, d x, there is nothing to hold, and the two mean the same.
add/upstream: Gradients flow backward, from the output toward the inputs. So the output's side is upstream, where the flow comes from, as on a river, and two is called the upstream gradient.
add/nudge: Now nudge x instead: three becomes three point zero one. q moves by the same hundredth, so the add's local slope for x is one, and f again moves two hundredths.
add/dx: So partial f, partial x, called d x in the code, is the local slope times the gradient from above: one times two, two.
add/copy: z is the same: q moves one for one with it. So an add gate copies the gradient from above, unchanged, to both inputs. Each gets the full two, not half of it.
mul/gate: A multiply gate is different. Now q is x times z: three times minus four, minus twelve. Again, two arrives from above.
mul/nudge: Nudge x up a hundredth, making it three point zero one, and q becomes minus twelve point zero four: it moves minus four times the nudge. So the local slope for x is z's value, minus four.
mul/dx: Then x gets minus four times the gradient from above: minus four times two, minus eight.
mul/dz: Nudge z instead, and q moves three times the nudge: the slope for z is x's value, three. So z gets three times two, six.
mul/rule: Each input gets the other input's value, times the gradient from above. The multiply gate swaps.
max/gate: A max gate passes on the larger of its inputs. With x three and z five, q is five.
max/x: Nudge x up a hundredth, making it three point zero one, and q stays five: z is still larger. The slope for x is zero, so x gets nothing.
max/z: Nudge z up a hundredth, making it five point zero one, and q moves with it: a slope of one. So z, the larger input, gets all of the two.
max/router: Add copies, multiply swaps, and max routes: the winner takes the whole gradient, and the other input gets nothing.
